new.definition: A loose skinned mandarin, Citrus unshiu, sweet, mild and usually seedless, whose peel slips off by hand and whose segments part cleanly. It is one of the most cold hardy citrus a Gulf Coast grower can plant, which is why it suits south Louisiana, where it is the leading citrus crop. The fruit ripens in the fall, from late September into early December depending on the variety, and Owari is the variety most widely grown.
new.guest: A satsuma is a sweet, easy peeling mandarin, and it is the citrus of a south Louisiana fall: the fruit comes in just as the weather turns. Its bright, gentle sweetness is set against the crisp, gently bitter endive and a cherry vinaigrette.
new.kitchen: The peel comes away by hand and the segments separate without a knife, so the fruit can be segmented close to service and stay juicy. How the salad's satsuma is cut, and whether it is Louisiana grown, are lineup questions.
new.compare: The navel orange, Louisiana's other citrus of the season, is its nearest neighbor: a navel is larger, with a tight, thick peel that wants a knife or a firm thumb, while a satsuma is smaller and its loose skin slips off in the hand.

new.background: The satsuma, Citrus unshiu, may have come from China, but it was first reported in Japan more than 700 years ago. The first recorded introduction to the United States was in Florida in 1876. Its English name is credited to the wife of an American minister to Japan, who sent trees home in 1878 from Satsuma, a former province that is now Kagoshima Prefecture. Between 1908 and 1911 about a million Owari satsuma trees were imported from Japan and planted along the lower Gulf Coast, from northern Florida to Texas, and they built a mandarin industry across the region. In Louisiana the satsuma, hardier in a freeze than most citrus, came to dominate the state's citrus plantings, and southern Plaquemines Parish, below New Orleans, is the center of the crop.

new.definition: The seeds of the common sunflower, Helianthus annuus, a plant native to North America. Seed grown to be eaten, called confection seed, is larger and striped, with a thick hull and less oil than the seed grown for pressing. For cooking the hull is cracked away and the kernel used, raw or roasted. Roasting turns the kernel golden and gives it a nutty, toasty flavor and a soft crunch.
new.guest: These are roasted sunflower seeds, the shelled kernels, toasted until golden. They bring a nutty, savory crunch to the salad, against the crisp endive and the juicy satsuma.
new.kitchen: Kernels are toasted dry, in the oven or a pan, until golden and fragrant, then cooled before they go on so they stay crisp. Whether they are salted or seasoned is the kitchen's to say, and every seed question goes to the kitchen.
new.compare: Pumpkin seeds, or pepitas, are the nearest neighbor on a salad: flat, oval and green, larger and softer to the bite, where a sunflower kernel is small and slim and roasts from gray to golden.

new.background: The common sunflower is one of the few crops first domesticated in what is now the United States. Genetic studies point to a single domestication in eastern North America, by its native peoples, long before Europeans arrived. Seed sent to Europe was grown mostly as a curiosity and a garden flower, and it was Russia that made the sunflower a field crop. Sunflower oil was not on the list of oily foods the Russian Orthodox Church restricted in Lent, which helped it spread, and by the nineteenth century it was grown across the Russian plains. Russian immigrants are thought to have carried its seed back to North America, and by the 1880s seed companies in the United States were offering a variety sold as Mammoth Russian.

new.definition: A cold sauce of oil and an acid, usually vinegar, whisked with salt and pepper, often with a little mustard to help it hold. The usual starting point is about three parts oil to one of vinegar, adjusted by taste for the oil and vinegar in hand. Whisking breaks the oil into tiny droplets through the vinegar, a temporary emulsion that separates as it stands and is whisked again before use. Flavored vinaigrettes add fruit, herbs, shallot or garlic.
new.guest: A vinaigrette is a light dressing of oil and vinegar whisked together, bright and sharp. Ours is a cherry vinaigrette, so it brings sweet, tart red fruit to the bitter endive and the satsuma.
new.kitchen: Whisked or shaken just before it dresses the leaves, because it separates as it stands, and tasted for balance; the salad is dressed at the last moment so the leaves stay crisp. What goes into the cherry vinaigrette beyond cherry is the kitchen's to say.
new.compare: Mayonnaise is its nearest neighbor among emulsified sauces: egg yolk holds a mayonnaise in a thick, lasting emulsion, while a vinaigrette has no yolk, stays pourable and separates as it stands.

new.background: Vinaigrette is the diminutive of the French vinaigre, vinegar, a word that itself means sour wine. The word is older than the dressing: in Le Viandier, a French cookbook of the fourteenth century, it names a meat dish, not a cold sauce. The modern sense was printed in the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française in 1694, which described a cold sauce of vinegar, oil, salt, pepper, parsley and chives. English took the word at the end of the seventeenth century, and John Evelyn (1620 to 1706) used it in Acetaria, his book on salads, in 1699. In nineteenth century American cookbooks, French dressing meant this plain dressing of oil and vinegar. In classical French cooking a vinaigrette dresses salads and, as a cold sauce, goes with artichokes, asparagus and leeks.

new.definition: A filled pasta of Piedmont in northwest Italy, made by folding a sheet or strip of pasta over small mounds of filling and pressing it shut, so each piece has a fold along one edge. The classic Piedmontese filling is roasted meat, pork and veal, first made to use up the leftovers of a roast. The small pinched kind are agnolotti del plin, plin meaning pinch in Piedmontese. Vegetable fillings, such as sweet potato, are modern variations on the shape.
new.guest: Agnolotti are a filled pasta from Piedmont in northern Italy, made by folding one sheet of pasta over the filling and pressing it closed. Ours are filled with sweet potato and finished in brown butter with candied pecans and goat cheese: the flavors of the holiday in an Italian shape.
new.kitchen: The pasta is rolled thin, the filling piped along it, the sheet folded over and sealed and the pieces cut, then cooked briefly in salted water and finished in the pan with the sauce. What is in the filling beyond sweet potato is a lineup question.
new.compare: Ravioli are the nearest neighbor: ravioli are often made by sealing a filling between two sheets of pasta, while agnolotti fold one sheet over it, so one edge of each piece is a fold. Agnolotti del plin are the small pinched form of the same pasta.

new.background: Agnolotti belong to Piedmont, in the northwest of Italy, and especially to the Monferrato hills and the country around Alessandria and Asti. They began as a thrifty dish, a way to use the leftover meat of a roast, and in Monferrato and Turin the classic filling is still roast pork and veal. Where the name comes from is not settled. One story credits a Monferrato cook called Angelot, or Angiolino, with the first of them; another ties the word to the Latin anulus, a ring, for the round shape of early agnolotti. The cook is told as legend, and no record settles the word. The small pinched form, agnolotti del plin, takes its name from plin, the Piedmontese word for a pinch, for the pinch of the fingers that seals each little parcel.

new.definition: The nut of Carya illinoinensis, a hickory whose native range centers on the lower Mississippi valley and reaches into Mexico, so Louisiana lies within it and the tree grows wild there. The kernel is rich, buttery and sweet, high in oil, and it toasts quickly. Native Louisiana pecans are smaller than the improved varieties, with a high oil content and full flavor. In Louisiana the harvest begins in October and runs toward Christmas, so the new crop arrives with the holidays.
new.guest: Pecans are native to this part of the country and grow wild in Louisiana; the new crop comes in each fall, just in time for the holidays. Here they are candied, sweet and crunchy, on the sweet potato agnolotti with brown butter and goat cheese.
new.kitchen: Toasted gently, because their oil scorches fast, and candied pecans are cooled until crisp before they go on the plate. Every nut question goes to the kitchen and the service note.
new.compare: The walnut is its nearest neighbor, a cousin in the same family: a pecan is longer and smoother, sweeter and more buttery, while a walnut is rounder and wrinkled, with a more bitter, tannic skin.

new.background: The word pecan came into English through the French of the Mississippi valley, pacane, from an Algonquian word for a nut, often glossed as a nut that needs a stone to crack. The tree is native to the Mississippi valley and south into Mexico, and its nuts were gathered long before Europeans arrived. A pecan does not grow true from seed. In the winter of 1846 an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, Louisiana, grafted cuttings of a fine wild tree onto other trees, and his grafts became the Centennial, named after its nuts were shown at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876, the first pecan variety known to have been propagated by grafting. In nineteenth century New Orleans, cooks put pecans in place of the almonds of the French praline and added cream, and the pecan praline became a New Orleans candy.

deepen.background: Belgian endive is a chicory grown twice: once in the field for its root, then again in the dark, where the lifted root sends up a tight, pale head. The Flemish call it witloof, white leaf, and French speaking Belgians call it chicon. A popular story says a farmer near Brussels hid his chicory roots in a dark cellar during the Belgian revolution of 1830 and later found white shoots on them, but Belgian accounts treat that as legend. The method is usually credited to a head gardener of the Brussels Botanical Garden, who forced chicory roots in the dark, probably building on what local growers already knew; accounts date his work anywhere from about 1830 to the 1840s. The crop spread through Schaerbeek, Evere and Haren, around Brussels, mainly in the second half of the nineteenth century.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Endive Satsuma Salad
deepen.guest: Endive is a crisp leaf of the chicory family with a gentle bitterness that wakes up the palate before a rich meal. In our salad the sweet satsuma and the cherry vinaigrette round off that bitterness, and roasted sunflower seeds add crunch.

deepen.background: Chèvre is the French word for goat, and in France fromage de chèvre, goat cheese, is a family of its own. Several of France's protected goat cheeses come from the Loire Valley, among them Sainte-Maure de Touraine, Selles-sur-Cher, Valençay and Crottin de Chavignol, and from Poitou to the south comes Chabichou du Poitou, protected since 1990. A legend says the region's goats were left behind by the Umayyad army after its defeat near Poitiers in 732, but goats were kept there long before, and the story is told as legend more than history. In the United States, nearly all the goat cheese sold was imported from Europe, much of it from France, until about 1980. In the late 1970s and early 1980s small farmstead makers in Northern California began making fresh chèvre, restaurants put it on their salads, and that work helped start the American specialty cheese movement.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: Sweet Potato Agnolotti
deepen.guest: Chèvre is French for goat, and here it means goat cheese: soft, white and gently tangy. On the sweet potato agnolotti its tang balances the sweet filling, the brown butter and the candied pecans.
